claims.text: Program.cs configures AddJwtBearer with ValidateIssuer, ValidateAudience, ValidateIssuerSigningKey and ValidateLifetime set to true, ValidIssuer/ValidAudience from Jwt:Issuer/Jwt:Audience, and IssuerSigningKey from Jwt:SigningKey.
Program.cs registers app.UseAuthentication() before app.UseAuthorization(), both before app.MapControllers().

The authentication middleware establishes the user from the token (or leaves the request unauthenticated) but does not reject requests itself; rejection of an [Authorize] endpoint happens in the authorization middleware, which challenges and the JwtBearer handler answers 401.

claims.text: OrdersController.List is marked [Authorize] and reads the caller's id from the sub claim via User.FindFirstValue(JwtRegisteredClaimNames.Sub).
401 means the request lacks valid authentication credentials; 403 means the server understood the request and refuses it, so sending the same caller's credentials again changes nothing.
A 401 response carries a WWW-Authenticate header naming the scheme (here Bearer), optionally with error="invalid_token" when a token was presented but rejected.
With no ClockSkew set, lifetime validation allows about five minutes of leeway: live, exp 60 s and 290 s in the past still got 200, exp 310 s in the past got 401.
claims.source_hint: TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew API docs (default 300 s); live run with tokens signed by the lab dev key

claims.text: ValidateIssuerSigningKey turns on validation of the signing key itself; the signature is verified against IssuerSigningKey regardless, so any token signed with that key passes the signature check.

claims.text: HTTP header field names are case-insensitive, so Www-Authenticate as printed by curl through Caddy is the same header as WWW-Authenticate.
